title: When the Glasshouse Falls
premise: Beatrix Eriksen, a night librarian who catalogs silences the way others catalog books, discovers a box of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe in the glasshouse-adjacent house she inherited from her estranged aunt. The letters, written over thirty years by four different hands, reveal a buried injustice: a wrongful eviction that scattered an improvised family and left one member erased from every record. As the deadline of the house sale looms, Beatrix tracks down the letter writers' surviving kin, learning that justice sometimes must be built by hand—through testimony, restitution, and witness—when courts and archives have failed. The novel ends with Beatrix delivering the final letter to its intended recipient, now elderly, on the glasshouse's last day before demolition, choosing found family over invisibility.
about_author: Coral Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging unclaimed property in municipal storage, where she first encountered boxes of letters no one ever came for. She writes at night, in libraries, about the quiet violence of things left unsaid.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. We meet her nocturnal routine: shelving returned books, logging overheard confessions in a private notebook, keeping the city's insomniacs company without engaging. A solicitor's letter arrives announcing the sale of Aunt Vera's house in three weeks. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness, the comfort of being unseen beginning to feel like erasure.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Clearing the house alone, she moves the wardrobe in Vera's back room and finds a tin box: forty-one undelivered letters spanning 1989–2022, none opened, addressed to people named only by initials. The last is dated two days before Vera's death. Emotional beat: vertigo—the discovery that the woman she mourned was a stranger.

chapters.title: What the Glasshouse Grew
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, interleaved with the first letter (from 'M'). Flashback texture: Vera ran the derelict municipal glasshouse as an unofficial refuge for runaways and evictees until it was condemned. Beatrix realizes she was born into this story. Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance; curiosity overriding grief.

chapters.title: Initials
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At the library she cross-references names against old news microfilm: a 1994 eviction scandal at the Fenwick Glasshouse, one resident, 'R. Okafor,' arrested for arson he likely didn't commit. The letters may be evidence never submitted. Emotional beat: the thrill and dread of holding something that could change a life.

chapters.title: The Man Who Slept in Aisles
chapters.summary: POV shift: Marisol, a retired tram driver and former glasshouse resident, now living in a care home. Beatrix visits under a false pretext. Marisol recognizes Vera's handwriting instantly and goes silent for a full minute. Emotional beat: guarded hope; the past is not past for everyone.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Her memory of the glasshouse's unwritten constitution: everyone cooks once, no one asks about yesterday, and Vera keeps the letters 'until they're safe to send.' We learn why some were never sent—fear, shame, one letter that could have freed Rudi but arrived too late to matter legally. Emotional beat: tenderness braided with guilt.

chapters.title: A Buyer with Clean Hands
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The developer pushing the sale, Callum Reeve, turns out to be the grandson of the councilman who ordered the eviction. He offers Beatrix a fast, generous close. She notices he flinches at the word 'glasshouse.' Emotional beat: moral temptation dressed as kindness.

chapters.title: The Arson File
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. In the records office she pulls the 1994 case file: Rudi Okafor served six years, died in 2011, record never expunged. But the fire report contradicts the conviction timeline—and letter #17, from 'T,' describes seeing the real cause. Emotional beat: cold anger at how paperwork outlives truth.

chapters.title: Letter Seventeen
chapters.summary: Tam's POV via the letter itself, read aloud in Beatrix's flat to Marisol. Tam, then fifteen, watched a faulty electrical junction ignite and was paid by the councilman's office to stay quiet. The letter was written but never sent because Tam feared deportation. Emotional beat: the weight of a silence kept for thirty years.

chapters.title: Finding Tam
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Tam Nguyen now runs a plant nursery—the glasshouse trade learned in exile. He refuses at first: 'I built a life on top of that grave.' His daughter, however, overhears and demands the truth. Emotional beat: confrontation between survival and conscience.

chapters.title: The Daughter Who Asked
chapters.summary: Linh's POV. She researches Rudi Okafor independently and finds his sister, Adaeze, still alive, still petitioning annually to clear her brother's name. Linh contacts her without telling Tam. Emotional beat: generational rupture as an engine of repair.

chapters.title: Adaeze
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Thirty years of petitions, each rejected on procedural grounds. When Linh's email arrives with scans of the letters, Adaeze weeps—not for vindication but because strangers remembered her brother's laugh. Emotional beat: grief finally given somewhere to go.

chapters.title: What Vera Knew
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Among the letters she finds Vera's own unsent draft: a confession that she withheld letter #17 in 1994, believing sending it would expose Tam to deportation, and chose Rudi's freedom over Tam's safety. Emotional beat: Beatrix's idolization of Vera collapses into complicated love.

chapters.title: Three Weeks Becomes Ten Days
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Reeve accelerates the sale, sensing bad publicity. Beatrix requests a stay citing potential historical significance; the council stalls. Marisol offers to testify; Tam wavers; Linh pushes. Emotional beat: the clock becomes a character, tightening every scene.

chapters.title: The Night Librarian Speaks
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. For the first time she breaks her own rule and tells her story publicly—at a library open-mic, reading letter #17 aloud anonymously. It spreads. Two other former residents come forward. Emotional beat: terror, then the strange lightness of being witnessed.

chapters.title: Reeve's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Callum's POV. Confronted by journalists and his own mother's diary confirming his grandfather's cover-up, Callum faces a choice: bury the story or fund the exoneration. He chooses, imperfectly, to delay the sale and pay for legal counsel. Emotional beat: inherited guilt meeting individual agency.

chapters.title: Hearing
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, courtroom scenes braided together. Adaeze testifies; Tam, hands shaking, reads his own words from 1994; Marisol describes the glasshouse family. The conviction is referred for posthumous review. Emotional beat: justice arriving small, procedural, and still enormous.

chapters.title: The Letter That Waited
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. With the case reopened, the remaining letters can finally be delivered. She spends nights hand-delivering them, each recipient a small resurrection. One addressee has died; Beatrix leaves the letter with his granddaughter, who reads it aloud. Emotional beat: mourning and mending in the same gesture.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The review will take years; the building will not wait. Reeve offers a compromise: preserve the glasshouse facade within the development if the community can show it matters. Beatrix must decide whether to fight for bricks or let them fall. Emotional beat: learning that memory lives in people, not structures.

chapters.title: Last Light Through Glass
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. On the final day, the found family gathers in the glasshouse: Marisol, Tam, Linh, Adaeze, Callum awkwardly holding a folding chair. They plant seedlings from Tam's nursery in the old beds and carry them out before the machines come. Emotional beat: elegy transformed into propagation.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She delivers the last letter—to Rudi Okafor himself, written by Vera the week before her death, asking his forgiveness. Adaeze accepts it on his behalf and asks Beatrix to read it at the memorial. Beatrix speaks her aunt's name fully, in daylight. Emotional beat: the inventory of unsaid things, finally emptied.

chapters.title: New Catalogue
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, epilogue. A year later: the exoneration is official, the glasshouse facade houses a public archive of the residents' letters, and Beatrix hosts a monthly night gathering there. Her notebook of unsaid things sits open on the desk, mostly blank now. Final line lands on her writing one new entry: a letter she intends to send. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope.
